title: Henry J. Grayson at Melbourne: surviving microscope test rulings, custody inscriptions, standards and ruling-engine afterlife

principal_upgrade.previous_state: Grayson was retained mainly as a methodological control: ruling instruments and photographs survived, while his research notebooks and papers were reported destroyed after his death.
principal_upgrade.new_state: The Ed Muirhead Physics Museum exposes multiple surviving Grayson microscope test rulings with maker inscriptions, exact line-density addresses, wrappers preserving custody history, and later museum identifiers. The case therefore supports an object-level maker -> ruled reference object -> custody/re-addressing chain even though the maker's research paper archive was lost.

diffraction_engine.guard: This is the later diffraction-grating engine. It is not evidence that identifier 35 produced microscope test plate 42. Grayson's earlier micro-ruling machine must be treated separately.

historical_context.biographical_source: Australian Dictionary of Biography, Henry Joseph Grayson
facts: Grayson made biological and petrological microscope slides before becoming internationally known for test rulings.
He constructed a new micro-ruling machine; an early form was largely glass and wood and produced lines to about 40,000 per inch.
William Stone designed and made central components for an improved form.
Carl Zeiss commissioned a plate with rulings up to 120,000 per inch to test Abbe's theory; Grayson exhibited rulings from 5,000 to 120,000 per inch in 1894.
Grayson later developed a distinct diffraction-grating ruling engine.
After Grayson's death, Stone collected his research notes and papers, which were accidentally burnt; Lyle bought the micro-ruling machine and ruling engine from the estate.

research_mechanism.chain: maker -> ruled microscope reference object -> line-density address on glass/label -> personal custody inscriptions -> university museum identifier/display
research_mechanism.strong_claim: Grayson's archive did not vanish simply because his notebooks were destroyed. Some procedural and custodial information migrated onto the ruled objects, their wrappers, boxes, scales and later museum records.

comparison.Cole: A serial number stabilizes a publication slot even when a preparation is replaced.
comparison.Grayson: A calibrated band/line-density scale stabilizes an optical reference function, while wrappers and museum identifiers record successive custody of the physical test object.

critical_guards: Do not identify test plate 42 as the Carl Zeiss commission merely because both reach 120,000 lines per inch; a direct provenance or commission record is required.
Do not claim that the surviving diffraction engine identifier 35 made the microscope test plate; Grayson's micro-ruling and diffraction-grating machines are distinct.
Do not convert 'Dup. Beck. Retain.' into a Beck sale, ownership or commission without corroborating correspondence/catalogue evidence.
Do not attribute the eight-slide test box wholly to Grayson; the museum itself says 'Probably Grayson trials or William Stone'.
The destruction of Grayson's papers is itself part of the provenance history; later Stone/Holmes/McNeill records are downstream evidence, not substitutes for the lost maker notebooks.
next_bounded_actions: Locate the current museum record or accession history for Grayson's earlier micro-ruling machine and distinguish it formally from the later diffraction engine.
Search Stone papers for identifiers or wording matching test plate 42, Grayson No. 2, 60,000, 120,000, Beck, or the Zeiss commission.
Search R. & J. Beck / Zeiss trade or correspondence records only against those exact inscriptions; no broad ruling-engine search is needed.
